questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A beekeeper groups areas that share the same soil type and climate. What kind of region is that?

options.misconception: confuses shared traits with networked activity
confuses objective traits with perceived identity
confuses soil region with city region

questions.explanation: A formal region is defined by uniform characteristics. The other region types rely on interaction or perception.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A newspaper serves a city and 4 surrounding counties. How many total counties make up its functional region?
questions.explanation: One city plus four surrounding counties equals five. The functional region is defined by the newspaper's reach.
questions.hint: Add the city county to the four.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: Residents call their area the Hill Country even though maps show no official boundary. What region type is that?
questions.explanation: Vernacular regions exist in people's perceptions and informal names. They lack official boundaries.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A beekeeper evaluates the physical traits of a plot: soil, slope, and sun exposure. What geographic concept is she assessing?

answer.exemplar: She is assessing the site, the physical characteristics of a place such as soil, slope, and climate.

questions.explanation: Site refers to physical characteristics. Situation refers to relative location instead.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY

stimulus.body: A beekeeper's apiary sits near a river, a road, and a city market. The logbook asks which concept describes its relative location.

questions.stem: Which concept describes the apiary's location relative to nearby features?

options.misconception: confuses relative location with physical traits

questions.explanation: Situation is relative location. Site would be the physical traits of the plot itself.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Distance at which two bid-rent curves meet
questions.stem: First, two land uses have bid-rent curves that cross at 3 kilometres from the centre. Second, what does that crossing point represent?

options.text: The boundary between the two land uses

questions.explanation: Where bid-rent curves cross, neither use outbids the other, so that distance marks their boundary.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A beekeeper notices market stalls spaced evenly along a road. Why do they appear at intervals rather than clustering?

options.text: Each stall needs a minimum customer base

questions.explanation: Each outlet needs a threshold population. Spacing reflects the minimum market area each can serve.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A region has 1 city, 3 towns, and 9 villages in its central place hierarchy. How many total settlements are there?
questions.explanation: One plus three plus nine equals thirteen settlements. The hierarchy nests smaller places under larger ones.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A beekeeper's shop draws customers from 10 kilometres away and needs 500 regular buyers to survive. Which term is the 10 kilometres?

options.misconception: confuses market reach with physical traits
confuses market reach with relative location

questions.explanation: Range is the maximum distance customers travel. Threshold is the minimum demand needed.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Ranking settlements by the goods they offer
questions.stem: A beekeeper ranks her town above a village because it offers more goods and services. What principle supports that ranking?

answer.exemplar: Larger settlements offer a wider range of goods and services, so ranking by goods offered reflects central place hierarchy.

questions.explanation: Central place theory links settlement size to the range of goods offered. Larger places serve larger market areas.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY

stimulus.body: A beekeeper studies the physical layout of streets, blocks, and buildings in her city. The logbook calls this urban morphology.

questions.stem: What does urban morphology examine?

options.text: The population growth rate of a city
The economic base of a city
The physical form and structure of a city

questions.explanation: Urban morphology studies physical form. Population, economy, and climate are different urban topics.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: First, land rent falls as distance from the centre increases. Second, what does this gradient explain?

options.text: Why all land uses cluster at the centre
Why different land uses locate at different distances
Why rent is zero at the edge

questions.explanation: The rent gradient sorts land uses by ability to pay. Different uses outbid each other at different distances.
questions.hint: Rent sorts land uses by distance.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Water left for allocation after an ecological reserve
questions.stem: A watershed yields 1,000 litres and an ecological reserve requires 300 litres. How much water remains for allocation?
questions.explanation: One thousand minus three hundred equals seven hundred litres remaining. The reserve must be set aside first.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What decides a land use boundary
questions.stem: Two competing land uses meet where their rents are equal. If one use pays 5 dollars more per hectare, how many hectares can it outbid the other?
questions.explanation: The question is conceptual; a 5 dollar advantage means it can outbid on one additional hectare at the margin. The value is one hectare.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A beekeeper compares the concentric zone and sector models. Which feature distinguishes the sector model?
questions.explanation: The sector model uses wedges shaped by transport routes. Concentric rings describe the zone model.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Sector model against observed land use
questions.stem: A city's industrial corridor follows a rail line in a wedge shape. Which land use model fits best?

answer.exemplar: The sector model fits best because industry follows the transport corridor in a wedge radiating from the centre.

questions.explanation: Industry aligning with transport in a wedge matches the sector model. Concentric rings would not show this corridor.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Land consumed by a dispersed pattern

stimulus.body: A beekeeper's dispersed settlement uses 2 hectares per household across 50 households.

questions.stem: How much total land is consumed?
questions.explanation: Two hectares times fifty households equals one hundred hectares. The dispersed pattern consumes more land.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: First, a city expands outward with low density. Second, what term describes that pattern?
questions.explanation: Low-density outward expansion is sprawl. Compact growth concentrates development instead.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why agglomeration pays and what it charges
questions.stem: Firms cluster to share labour and suppliers, but face higher rents. What concept captures both effects?
questions.explanation: Agglomeration brings benefits like shared inputs and costs like higher rents. Both sides belong to the concept.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why a watershed is a management unit
questions.stem: A watershed collects runoff from 4 sub-basins. How many sub-basins drain into it?
questions.explanation: All four sub-basins drain into the watershed. Managing the whole unit protects downstream water.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A common pasture is overgrazed because each herder gains full benefit but shares the cost. What problem is this?

options.misconception: names the limit, not the failure

questions.explanation: The tragedy of the commons occurs when individual incentives deplete a shared resource. Carrying capacity is the limit, not the problem.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Sustainable offtake from a regenerating resource
questions.stem: A forest regenerates 100 cubic metres per year. What is the sustainable annual harvest?

answer.exemplar: The sustainable annual harvest equals the regeneration rate, so 100 cubic metres per year can be taken without depleting the stock.

questions.explanation: Sustainable offtake cannot exceed regeneration. Taking exactly the regeneration rate keeps stock constant.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY

stimulus.body: A fishery collapses when harvests exceed the stock's ability to regenerate. The logbook asks what concept names the maximum sustainable harvest.

questions.stem: Which concept names the maximum sustainable harvest?

options.misconception: confuses sustainable limit with market distance
confuses sustainable limit with minimum demand
confuses sustainable limit with land value

questions.explanation: Carrying capacity is the maximum sustainable use. Threshold, range, and bid rent describe other concepts.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: First, a thinker claims climate alone dictates how societies develop. Second, what is that view called?

options.misconception: confuses climate view with perceived region

questions.explanation: Environmental determinism holds that environment controls human outcomes. Possibilism allows human choice instead.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why climate zones do not have sharp edges
questions.stem: A beekeeper observes forest gradually turning to grassland with no sharp line. What explains the gradual change?
questions.explanation: Climate and vegetation change gradually across space, creating ecotones rather than sharp edges.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A flood hazard affects 3 communities, 2 are exposed, and 1 is vulnerable. How many communities are exposed?
questions.explanation: Two communities are exposed. Hazard, exposure, and vulnerability are distinct concepts.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: The vulnerable share of an exposed population
questions.stem: Among 1,000 exposed people, 200 are vulnerable. What share is vulnerable?
questions.explanation: Two hundred divided by one thousand equals 20 percent. The share uses exposed population as denominator.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A beekeeper installs flood barriers and also reduces emissions. Which action is mitigation and which is adaptation?

answer.exemplar: Reducing emissions is mitigation because it lessens the hazard, while flood barriers are adaptation because they reduce vulnerability to flooding.

questions.explanation: Mitigation reduces causes of change. Adaptation reduces harm from change.
questions.hint: Mitigation cuts causes; adaptation cuts harm.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A barrier against ten years of flood damage

stimulus.body: A beekeeper builds a levee rated for a 10-year flood. The logbook asks what that rating means.

questions.stem: What does a 10-year flood rating imply?

options.text: A flood of that size has a 10 percent annual chance

questions.explanation: A 10-year flood has a 10 percent chance each year. It is not a schedule or a guarantee.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: First, Country A has a larger total emission but lower per-capita emission than Country B. Second, which is more populous?
questions.explanation: Larger total with lower per-capita implies larger population. Country A must be more populous.
questions.hint: Total divided by per-capita gives population.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A country releases 500 million tonnes across 50 million people. What is the per-capita release?
questions.explanation: Five hundred million divided by fifty million equals ten tonnes per person.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: Country X emits 8 tonnes per person and Country Y emits 12 tonnes per person. How many tonnes more per person does Y emit?
questions.explanation: Twelve minus eight equals four tonnes more per person. The difference is a simple subtraction.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A beekeeper labels an area by its uniform language and religion. Which region type is that?

options.misconception: relies on perception, not uniform traits

questions.explanation: Uniform cultural traits define a formal region. The other types rely on interaction or perception.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A region named only by its residents
questions.stem: An area has no official name but locals all call it the Valley. What region type is that?

answer.exemplar: It is a vernacular region, defined by residents' perceptions and informal names rather than official boundaries.

questions.explanation: Vernacular regions exist in people's minds and informal usage. They lack formal designation.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: One city block, two different sites

stimulus.body: Two adjacent plots on the same block have different soil and slope but identical access to roads and markets.

questions.stem: Which concept differs between the two plots?

options.misconception: confuses relative location with physical traits
confuses physical traits with market distance
confuses physical traits with minimum demand

questions.explanation: Soil and slope are physical site traits. Access to roads and markets is situation, which is identical here.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A ridge that silts up and a route that moves
questions.stem: First, a river ridge silts up and a trade route shifts to a new channel. Second, what geographic process does this illustrate?

options.misconception: confuses river shift with city form
confuses the route shift with site change

options.text: Changing situation due to physical change

questions.explanation: The route's relative location changes because the physical ridge changed. Situation shifts with physical change.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A common pasture with a new road through it
questions.stem: A new road through a common pasture increases access and grazing pressure. What risk rises?

options.text: Decreased carrying capacity of the road

questions.explanation: Greater access can increase overuse of the commons. The shared resource faces depletion risk.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why mitigation and adaptation are not substitutes
questions.stem: A plan reduces emissions by 30 percent and builds levees for the rest. How many percent of risk is addressed by adaptation?
questions.explanation: If mitigation covers 30 percent, adaptation addresses the remaining 70 percent. The two complement rather than substitute.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why the top-down map is misleading
questions.stem: A top-down map shows a region as uniform. Why might that mislead a beekeeper?
questions.explanation: Top-down views smooth over local differences. The beekeeper needs ground-level detail.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A beekeeper relies only on levees to manage flood risk. Why might that approach fail?

answer.exemplar: Levees alone fail when floods exceed their design level or when upstream changes increase runoff, so adaptation needs backup measures.

questions.explanation: Protection has design limits and can create false security. Combined strategies are safer.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY

stimulus.body: A beekeeper maps areas with identical rainfall and temperature. The logbook asks what region type results.

questions.stem: What region type results from uniform climate?
questions.explanation: Uniform climate defines a formal region. Interaction or perception defines the others.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: First, a delivery service connects a hub to 6 spokes. Second, what region type is the service area?
questions.explanation: A networked service area is a functional region. Uniform traits or perception define the others.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: Locals call an area the Midlands though no map labels it. What region type is that?
questions.explanation: Informal local names define vernacular regions. The others need official or network criteria.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A plot has soil pH 6.5 and slope 5 degrees. How many site traits are listed?
questions.explanation: Soil pH and slope are two physical site traits. The count is straightforward.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A beekeeper's plot is 2 km from a road and 5 km from a market. Which concept do these distances describe?

options.misconception: confuses relative distances with physical traits

questions.explanation: Distances to roads and markets are relative location, or situation. Site would be physical traits.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Distance at which two bid-rent curves meet
questions.stem: Two bid-rent curves cross at 4 km from the centre. What is the boundary distance?

answer.exemplar: The boundary between the two land uses is 4 kilometres from the centre, where their bid rents are equal.

questions.explanation: The crossing point marks where neither use outbids the other, fixing the boundary at 4 km.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY

stimulus.body: A beekeeper observes market stalls evenly spaced along a highway. The logbook asks why they are not clustered.

questions.stem: Why are the stalls evenly spaced?

options.text: Each needs a minimum market area

questions.explanation: Even spacing reflects the minimum market area each stall needs. The other options overstate or misstate the cause.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: First, a village offers groceries and a town offers groceries plus a hospital. Second, which settlement is higher in the hierarchy?
questions.explanation: The town offers more services, so it ranks higher in the central place hierarchy.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A service needs 300 customers to survive and draws them from 8 km away. Which number is the threshold?
questions.explanation: Threshold is the minimum demand, 300 customers. Range is the distance, 8 km.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Ranking settlements by the goods they offer
questions.stem: A city offers 20 goods, a town offers 12, and a village offers 5. How many more goods does the city offer than the town?
questions.explanation: Twenty minus twelve equals eight more goods. The difference reflects the hierarchy.
questions.hint: Subtract town goods from city goods.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A beekeeper studies street grids and block shapes. What field is she working in?
questions.explanation: Street grids and block shapes are physical form, studied by urban morphology.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: Land rent is highest at the centre and falls outward. What pattern does this create?

answer.exemplar: It creates an urban gradient where land uses sort by ability to pay, with highest-value uses near the centre.

questions.explanation: The gradient sorts uses by rent-paying ability, concentrating high-value uses centrally.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Water left for allocation after an ecological reserve

stimulus.body: A watershed yields 800 litres and an ecological reserve requires 200 litres. The logbook asks how much remains for allocation.

questions.stem: How much water remains for allocation?
questions.explanation: Eight hundred minus two hundred equals six hundred litres remaining.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What decides a land use boundary
questions.stem: First, two land uses compete for the same location. Second, where does one replace the other?

options.text: Where their bid rents are equal

questions.explanation: The boundary occurs where neither use outbids the other, so bid rents are equal.
questions.hint: Equal bid rents mark the boundary.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A city's land use appears as concentric rings around the centre. Which model is that?
questions.explanation: Concentric rings describe the zone model. Sectors need transport wedges, and multiple nuclei need several centres.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Sector model against observed land use
questions.stem: A sector extends 3 km along a road and 2 km perpendicular. What is its approximate area in square kilometres?
questions.explanation: Three times two equals six square kilometres. The sector area is a simple product.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Land consumed by a dispersed pattern
questions.stem: A dispersed suburb uses 0.5 hectares per house across 100 houses. How much land is consumed?
questions.explanation: Zero point five times one hundred equals fifty hectares. The dispersed pattern consumes substantial land.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.stem: A city grows by adding dense infill near the centre. What growth pattern is that?

answer.exemplar: That is compact growth, concentrating development in existing areas rather than spreading outward at low density.

questions.explanation: Dense infill near the centre is compact growth. Sprawl would spread outward at low density.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why agglomeration pays and what it charges

stimulus.body: Firms cluster to share workers and suppliers but pay higher rents. The logbook asks what concept names both sides.

questions.stem: What concept names both benefits and costs of clustering?
questions.explanation: Agglomeration includes both shared benefits and congestion costs. The other terms describe different concepts.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why a watershed is a management unit
questions.stem: First, rain falls across an entire drainage basin. Second, why manage the whole basin as one unit?
questions.explanation: Water flows link all parts of a basin, so managing the whole unit protects downstream quality and quantity.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used
